reminder: A complete quadrangle is four [points](c:point) of a [projective plane](c:projective-plane), no three [collinear](c:collinear-points), with the six lines through pairs of them.
definition: A complete quadrangle in a [projective plane](c:projective-plane) is a set of four [points](c:point), the vertices, no three of which lie on one [line](c:line), together with the six lines that join pairs of vertices, the sides. Two sides that share no vertex are opposite, and the three points where opposite sides meet are the diagonal points.
examples: The points $[1:0:0]$, $[0:1:0]$, $[0:0:1]$ and $[1:1:1]$ of the real projective plane form a complete quadrangle, and they are the standard [projective frame](c:projective-frame).
The four vertices of a convex quadrilateral in the real plane, with its four sides and two diagonals, form a complete quadrangle in the projective plane.
Non-example: the points $[1:0:0]$, $[0:1:0]$, $[1:1:0]$ and $[0:0:1]$ are not a complete quadrangle, because the first three lie on the line $z=0$.

reminder: A completion of an object is the smallest larger object that contains it and has a property that the object lacks.
definition: Given an object $C$ and a property $P$ that $C$ may lack, a completion of $C$ with respect to $P$ is an object $\hat C$ that has $P$, contains $C$ as a subobject, and is [universal](c:universal-property) for this: every suitable map from $C$ to an object with $P$ extends uniquely to $\hat C$. For [metric spaces](c:metric-space) and the property of being a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space), the suitable maps are the uniformly continuous ones.
examples: The real numbers are the completion of the rationals: every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) of rationals gets a limit, and the rationals stay [dense](c:dense-set).
The [p-adic numbers](c:p-adic-number) are the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for the $p$-adic absolute value.

Non-example: the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ contains $\mathbb{Q}$ isometrically as $\mathbb{Q}\times\{0\}$ and is complete, but it is not the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is not dense in it.

steps: Take a ring $R$ and a finitely generated ideal $I$, and ask that $R$ be complete in the $I$-adic topology.
Form $\hat R=\varprojlim R/I^n$ together with the canonical map $R\to\hat R$.
Then $\hat R$ is complete in the $I$-adic topology, and the image of $R$ is dense in it.
links.why: It shows that the ring completion is one case of the general recipe: embed densely into something with the missing property.

steps: Take a partially ordered set $P$ and ask for a complete lattice that contains $P$ as a subposet.
The MacNeille completion is a complete lattice in which $P$ keeps all its existing suprema and infima.
It is the smallest complete lattice with this property, so it is the completion of $P$ for being a complete lattice.
links.why: It shows that completing an order is the same idea as completing a metric space.

reminder: Complex projective space $\mathbb{C}P^n$ is the set of one-dimensional complex subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$.
definition: Complex projective space $\mathbb{C}P^n$ is the quotient of $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ by the relation $z\sim\lambda z$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$. It is the [projective space](c:projective-space) of dimension $n$ over the [complex numbers](c:complex-number), and it is a compact [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of complex dimension $n$ and real dimension $2n$.
examples: $\mathbb{C}P^0$ is a point, and $\mathbb{C}P^1$ is the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere), the complex line with one point at infinity.
$\mathbb{C}P^2$ is the set of complex lines through the origin of $\mathbb{C}^3$, a complex surface of real dimension $4$.
Non-example: the real projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$ is not complex projective space; it has real dimension $2$ but is not orientable, so it has no complex structure.

steps: Take the field $\mathbb{C}$ of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) as the base field.
Form the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$.
This set is the projective space of dimension $n$ over $\mathbb{C}$, and the complex case adds a complex manifold structure.
links.why: It shows that results about projective spaces over any field also hold for $\mathbb{C}P^n$.

steps: Start with $\mathbb{C}P^n$ for a natural number $n$.
Choose the value $n=2$ for the dimension.
Then $\mathbb{C}P^2$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^3$, which is the complex projective plane.
links.why: It shows that the complex projective plane is the case $n=2$ of a whole family.

reminder: Composing two [Markov kernels](c:markov-kernel) draws $y$ from the first kernel at $x$, then draws $z$ from the second kernel at $y$.
definition: Let $\kappa$ be a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) from a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ to $Y$, and let $\eta$ be a Markov kernel from $Y$ to $Z$. Their composition $\eta\circ\kappa$ is the Markov kernel from $X$ to $Z$ given by $(\eta\circ\kappa)(x,C)=\int_Y\eta(y,C)\,\kappa(x,dy)$ for $x\in X$ and measurable $C\subseteq Z$, where the [integral](c:integral) averages over the intermediate state $y$.
examples: On finite sets a kernel is a matrix of probabilities with row sums $1$, and the composition of kernels is the product of the matrices.
For a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) with transition kernels $p_s$ and $p_t$, the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation says $p_{s+t}=p_t\circ p_s$.

Non-example: for kernels on one space, the pointwise product $\kappa(x,C)\,\eta(x,C)$ is not the composition, and it is not even additive in $C$ when both kernels are uniform on two points, since the singletons get $1/4$ each and their union gets $1$.

steps: A Markov kernel from $X$ to $Y$ is the same as a measurable map from $X$ to the space of probability measures on $Y$.
This is a morphism from $X$ to $Y$ in the Kleisli category of the [Giry monad](c:giry-monad).
Kleisli composition pushes the measure $\kappa(x,\cdot)$ forward by $\eta$ and then averages with the monad multiplication, which is the integral formula.
So composition of kernels is composition in the Kleisli category of the Giry monad.
links.why: It shows that kernel composition is associative and unital for the same reason as every Kleisli composition.

reminder: A composition series of $M$ is a finite chain of submodules from $0$ up to $M$ whose successive quotients are all simple.
definition: A composition series of a [module](c:module) $M$ is a finite chain $0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_n=M$ of [submodules](c:submodule) such that each [quotient module](c:quotient-module) $M_i/M_{i-1}$ is a [simple module](c:is-simple-module). For a group, the same definition uses a chain of subgroups in which each is [normal](c:normal-subgroup) in the next and each quotient is a [simple group](c:simple-group).
examples: The group $S_3$ has the composition series $1\lhd A_3\lhd S_3$, with factors $\mathbb{Z}/3$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
The $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}/6$ has the series $0\subset\langle3\rangle\subset\mathbb{Z}/6$, with quotients $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/3$.

Non-example: the chain $0\subset2\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is not a composition series of $\mathbb{Z}$, because $2\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}$ is not simple; in fact $\mathbb{Z}$ has no composition series.

steps: A composition series is a finite chain of submodules $0=M_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_n=M$.
Such a chain is a finite [filtration](c:filtration) of $M$.
The composition series adds the condition that each successive quotient is simple, so no step of the chain can be refined.
links.why: It shows that a composition series is a filtration that cannot be refined.

steps: Let $G$ be a group with a composition series $1=G_0\lhd G_1\lhd\cdots\lhd G_n=G$.
Each $G_{i-1}$ is normal in $G_i$, so this chain is a [subnormal series](c:subnormal-series) of $G$.
The composition series adds the condition that every factor $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is simple.
links.why: It shows that a composition series is a subnormal series with simple factors.

reminder: A set of natural numbers is computable when some algorithm decides, for every number, whether it belongs to the set.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is computable, also called decidable, when its [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) $\chi_S:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\}$ is a [computable function](c:computable-function). Equivalently, some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) halts on every input $n$ and accepts exactly the $n$ that lie in $S$.
examples: The set of even numbers and the set of prime numbers are computable.
Every finite subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is computable.
Non-example: the halting set $K=\{e: \text{program } e \text{ halts on input } e\}$ is not computable, because a decider for $K$ would solve the [halting problem](c:halting-problem).

steps: Let $S$ be a computable set with a decider $D$ that halts on every input.
Run $D$ on $0,1,2,\dots$ in turn and list every $n$ that $D$ accepts.
This procedure lists exactly the elements of $S$, so $S$ is a [recursively enumerable set](c:recursively-enumerable-set).
The computable case adds that the complement of $S$ is also recursively enumerable.
links.why: It shows that a computable set is a recursively enumerable set whose complement is recursively enumerable too.

reminder: Two [random variables](c:random-variable) are conditionally independent given $Z$ when, once $Z$ is known, one gives no more information about the other.
definition: Random variables $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given a random variable $Z$ when $P(X\in A,\,Y\in B\mid Z)=P(X\in A\mid Z)\,P(Y\in B\mid Z)$ almost surely, for all measurable sets $A$ and $B$, where $P(\cdot\mid Z)$ is a [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability). More generally, one can condition on a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) in place of $Z$.
examples: Flip a coin with unknown bias $\theta$ twice: the two flips are conditionally independent given $\theta$, but they are not independent.
In a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain), the future $X_{n+1}$ and the past $X_{n-1}$ are conditionally independent given the present $X_n$.
Non-example: let $X$ and $Y$ be independent fair bits and $Z=X+Y$. Given $Z=1$ the bits are $X$ and $1-X$, so $X$ and $Y$ are not conditionally independent given $Z$.

steps: Take a constant random variable $Z$, which carries no information.
Conditioning on a constant changes no probability, so $P(\cdot\mid Z)=P(\cdot)$.
The defining equation becomes $P(X\in A,\,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)\,P(Y\in B)$.
This is the [independence](c:independent-random-variables) of $X$ and $Y$.
links.why: It shows that ordinary independence is conditional independence given no information.

reminder: The conductor of an abelian extension of number fields is the smallest modulus whose ray class field contains the extension.
definition: Let $L/K$ be an [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field). A modulus of $K$ is a formal product of finite primes with exponents and some real places, and the conductor $\mathfrak f(L/K)$ is the smallest modulus $\mathfrak m$ such that $L$ lies in the ray class field of $K$ modulo $\mathfrak m$. The places that divide $\mathfrak f(L/K)$ are exactly the places of $K$ that [ramify](c:ramification-of-ideals) in $L$.
examples: For $n\not\equiv2\pmod 4$, the finite part of the conductor of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}$ is $n$.
A quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$ has finite conductor $|D|$, where $D$ is its discriminant.
Non-example: the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ is not an abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, because it is not even Galois, so it has no conductor in this sense.

reminder: A congruence on a category is an equivalence relation on every set of morphisms that is compatible with composition.
definition: A congruence on a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is a family of [equivalence relations](c:equivalence-relation) $\sim$, one on each [hom-set](c:hom-set) $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$, such that $f\sim f'$ implies $g\circ f\sim g\circ f'$ and $f\circ h\sim f'\circ h$ whenever the [composites](c:composition) are defined. Then the classes of morphisms form the [quotient category](c:quotient) $\mathcal C/{\sim}$.
examples: Homotopy of continuous maps is a congruence on the category of topological spaces, and its quotient is the homotopy category.
A monoid is a one-object category, and a congruence on it is the usual monoid congruence, such as congruence modulo $n$ on $(\mathbb{N},+)$.

Non-example: on $(\mathbb{N},+)$ as a one-object category, the relation $\lfloor m/2\rfloor=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is an equivalence, but $0\sim1$ and $1+0\not\sim1+1$, so it is not compatible with composition.

steps: View a monoid $M$ as a category with one object, whose morphisms are the elements of $M$.
Composition is the product of $M$, so the only hom-set is $M$ itself.
A [congruence relation](c:con) on $M$ is an equivalence relation on $M$ that is compatible with the product on both sides.
This is exactly a congruence on the one-object category.
links.why: It shows that a congruence on a category is a monoid congruence with many objects.

reminder: A [graph](c:graph) is connected when every two [vertices](c:vertex) are joined by a [path](c:path).
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $G$ is connected when, for every two [vertices](c:vertex) $u$ and $v$, there is a [path](c:path) in $G$ from $u$ to $v$. By convention, a connected graph has at least one vertex.
examples: Every [complete graph](c:complete-graph) is connected, because any two vertices share an edge.
A [tree](c:tree) is connected, and so is a cycle.
Non-example: the graph with vertices $1,2,3,4$ and edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ is not connected, because no path joins $1$ to $3$.

steps: Start with a [tree](c:tree), which is a graph with no [cycle](c:cycle) in which every two vertices are joined by a path.
The path condition says that the tree is connected.
So every tree is a connected graph, and the tree adds only that the graph has no cycle.
links.why: It shows that a tree is a connected graph with no cycle.

steps: Start with a [complete graph](c:complete-graph), in which every two distinct vertices share an edge.
An edge is a path of length one, so any two vertices are joined by a path.
So a complete graph is connected, and it adds that all paths can be taken of length at most one.
links.why: It shows that a complete graph is the most strongly connected graph on its vertices.

reminder: A subset of a topological space is connected when it is not the union of two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $S$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is connected when $S$ with the [subspace topology](c:subspace-topology) is a [connected space](c:connected-space). That is, $S$ is not the union of two disjoint nonempty sets that are [open](c:open-set) in $S$.
examples: Every interval of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, and these are all the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
The unit circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is connected.
Non-example: $[0,1]\cup[2,3]\subset\mathbb{R}$ is not connected, because $[0,1]$ and $[2,3]$ are disjoint, nonempty and open in the subspace.

steps: Let $S$ be path connected and fix a point $p\in S$.
For each $x\in S$ choose a path from $p$ to $x$ in $S$; its image is connected because $[0,1]$ is connected.
These images all contain $p$, and a union of connected sets with a common point is connected.
The union is $S$, so $S$ is connected.
links.why: It shows that every path-connected set is connected, so path-connectedness is a stronger test.

reminder: A conservation law is an [observable](c:observable) whose value stays constant along every solution of a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system).
definition: A conservation law of a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system) is an [observable](c:observable) $Q$, a function on the states, such that $Q(x(t))$ does not depend on $t$ for every [solution](c:solution) $x(t)$. For a field theory, one often writes the law locally as a continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot J=0$, where $\rho$ is a density and $J$ is its flux.
examples: The total energy of a mechanical system with a time-independent Hamiltonian is constant along every solution.
The equation $\partial_tu+\partial_x(u^2/2)=0$ conserves $\int u\,dx$ when no flux leaves the region.
Non-example: the energy $E=\tfrac12\dot x^2+\tfrac12x^2$ of the damped oscillator $\ddot x=-x-\dot x$ is not conserved, because $\dot E=-\dot x^2<0$ whenever $\dot x\ne0$.

reminder: A [functor](c:functor) $F$ is conservative when it reflects isomorphisms, so $F(g)$ invertible forces $g$ invertible.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F:C\to D$ is conservative when every morphism $g$ of $C$ such that $F(g)$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) in $D$ is already an isomorphism in $C$. In other words, $F$ reflects isomorphisms.
examples: The forgetful functor from groups to sets is conservative, because a bijective group homomorphism has an inverse that is also a homomorphism.
Every fully faithful functor, such as the inclusion of a full subcategory, is conservative.
Non-example: the forgetful functor from topological spaces to sets is not conservative, because a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism, such as $[0,1)\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$.

steps: Let $F$ be fully faithful, and let $g:a\to b$ be a morphism such that $F(g)$ has an inverse $k$.
Because $F$ is full, there is a morphism $h:b\to a$ with $F(h)=k$.
Then $F(hg)=F(\mathrm{id}_a)$ and $F(gh)=F(\mathrm{id}_b)$, so faithfulness gives $hg=\mathrm{id}_a$ and $gh=\mathrm{id}_b$.
So $g$ is an isomorphism, and $F$ is conservative.
links.why: It shows that fully faithful functors never lose isomorphisms, so they are conservative.

steps: Let $U$ be monadic, so it is the forgetful functor from the algebras of a monad $T$ to the base category.
A morphism of $T$-algebras whose underlying morphism is an isomorphism has an inverse in the base category.
This inverse commutes with the algebra structures, so it is a morphism of algebras.
So the algebra morphism is an isomorphism, and $U$ is conservative.
links.why: It shows that every monadic functor reflects isomorphisms.

reminder: A continued fraction writes a number as $a_0+1/(a_1+1/(a_2+\cdots))$ with integer partial quotients.
definition: A simple continued fraction is an expression $[a_0;a_1,a_2,\dots]=a_0+1/(a_1+1/(a_2+\cdots))$ with $a_0\in\mathbb{Z}$ and positive integers $a_1,a_2,\dots$, the partial quotients; it is finite or infinite. A finite one represents a [rational number](c:rational-number), and an infinite one is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of its finite truncations, the convergents, taken along the [sequence](c:sequence) of partial quotients.
examples: The golden ratio is $[1;1,1,1,\dots]$, and $\sqrt2=[1;2,2,2,\dots]$.
Non-example: $1+1/(\tfrac12+1/3)$ is not a simple continued fraction, because $\tfrac12$ is not an integer.

reminder: A continuous linear equivalence is a [linear](c:linear-map) bijection between [topological vector spaces](c:topological-vector-space) that is continuous with continuous inverse.
definition: A continuous linear equivalence $E\to F$ between [topological vector spaces](c:topological-vector-space) is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T$ that is a [bijection](c:bijection) such that both $T$ and its inverse $T^{-1}$ are continuous. Equivalently, it is a [linear isomorphism](c:linear-isomorphism) that is also a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).
examples: Every invertible matrix is a continuous linear equivalence $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$, and so is every linear bijection between finite-dimensional normed spaces.
On a normed space, multiplication by a nonzero scalar $c$ is a continuous linear equivalence, with inverse multiplication by $1/c$.
Non-example: the identity map from $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm to $C[0,1]$ with the $L^1$ norm is a continuous linear bijection, but its inverse is not continuous.

steps: Let $T$ be a continuous linear equivalence $E\to F$.
Forget the linear structure and see $T$ as a map between topological spaces.
The map $T$ is a continuous bijection, and its inverse is continuous.
So $T$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), and the linear case adds that $T$ is linear.
links.why: It shows that topological facts about homeomorphisms apply to continuous linear equivalences.

steps: Let $T$ be a continuous linear equivalence $E\to F$.
Forget the topologies and keep only the vector space structure.
Then $T$ is a linear bijection, so it is a [linear isomorphism](c:linear-isomorphism).
The topological case adds that both $T$ and $T^{-1}$ are continuous.
links.why: It shows that a continuous linear equivalence is a linear isomorphism with two continuity conditions.

reminder: The contraction rule says that a [deduction](c:deduction) that uses a premise twice stays valid when it uses the premise only once.
definition: The contraction rule is a [structural rule](c:structural-rule) of a logic: if the [sequent](c:sequent) $\Gamma,A,A\vdash B$ is derivable, then $\Gamma,A\vdash B$ is derivable. A logic with contraction lets a proof use an assumption again and again.
examples: Classical and intuitionistic logic have contraction: from $A,A\vdash B$ one gets $A\vdash B$.
Contraction lets a proof of $A\to(A\wedge A)$ use the assumption $A$ twice.
Non-example: in [linear logic](c:linear-logic) the rule fails, so $A\vdash A\otimes A$ is not derivable; each assumption can be used only once.

reminder: A controlled gate applies a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) to its target qubits only when its control qubit is in the state $|1\rangle$.
definition: Given a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U$ on $n$ [qubits](c:qbit), the controlled-$U$ gate acts on $1+n$ qubits by $|0\rangle|\psi\rangle\mapsto|0\rangle|\psi\rangle$ and $|1\rangle|\psi\rangle\mapsto|1\rangle U|\psi\rangle$. As a matrix it is $|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U$ with a [tensor product](c:tensor-product), and with several control qubits the gate applies $U$ only when all of them are $|1\rangle$.
examples: The [CNOT gate](c:cnot-gate) is controlled-$X$: it sends $|a,b\rangle$ to $|a,a\oplus b\rangle$.
The controlled-$Z$ gate multiplies the state $|11\rangle$ by $-1$ and leaves the other basis states unchanged, and the Toffoli gate is controlled-controlled-$X$.
Non-example: the SWAP gate exchanges $|01\rangle$ and $|10\rangle$, so for neither qubit does it leave every state with that qubit in $|0\rangle$ unchanged; it is not a controlled gate.

steps: Let $U$ be a unitary on $n$ qubits and form $C(U)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U$.
The projectors $|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $|1\rangle\langle1|$ are orthogonal and sum to the identity.
So $C(U)^\dagger C(U)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U^\dagger U=I$, and $C(U)$ is unitary.
A unitary on qubits is a [quantum gate](c:quantum-gate), so $C(U)$ is a gate with the added control structure.
links.why: It shows that every controlled gate is a legal quantum gate when $U$ is unitary.

reminder: A convex cone is a subset of a real [vector space](c:vector-space) that is closed under addition and under multiplication by positive scalars.
definition: A subset $C$ of a real [vector space](c:vector-space) is a convex cone when $x+y\in C$ and $\lambda x\in C$ for all $x,y\in C$ and all real $\lambda>0$. The origin may or may not belong to $C$.
examples: The nonnegative orthant $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i\ge0\text{ for all }i\}$ is a convex cone.
The positive semidefinite matrices form a convex cone in the space of symmetric matrices.
Non-example: the closed unit ball is a [convex set](c:convex-set) but not a cone, because $2x$ leaves the ball when $\|x\|=1$.
Non-example: the union of the two coordinate axes of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is closed under positive scaling but not under addition, because $(1,0)+(0,1)$ is not in it.

steps: Let $C$ be a convex cone, let $x,y\in C$ and let $0<t<1$.
Then $tx$ and $(1-t)y$ lie in $C$, because both scalars are positive.
Their sum lies in $C$ by closure under addition, so $tx+(1-t)y\in C$.
The cases $t=0$ and $t=1$ give $y$ and $x$, so $C$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set).
links.why: It shows that every convex cone is convex, so results about convex sets apply to cones.

reminder: The covariance function of a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ is $K(s,t)=\mathrm{Cov}(X_s,X_t)$ for all times $s$ and $t$.
definition: For a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ with finite second moments, the covariance function is $K(s,t)=\mathbb{E}[(X_s-m(s))(X_t-m(t))]$, where $m(t)=\mathbb{E}[X_t]$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value). It is symmetric and it is a [positive definite kernel](c:positive-definite-kernel), which means $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(t_i,t_j)\ge0$ for all real numbers $c_i$.
examples: For [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion), the covariance function is $K(s,t)=\min(s,t)$.
For a [stationary process](c:stationary-process), $K(s,t)$ depends only on the difference $s-t$.
Non-example: $K(s,t)=s-t$ is not a covariance function, because it is not symmetric.

steps: Let $K(s,t)=\mathrm{Cov}(X_s,X_t)$, and choose times $t_1,\dots,t_n$ and real numbers $c_1,\dots,c_n$.
Put $Y=\sum_ic_i(X_{t_i}-m(t_i))$, so that $\mathbb{E}[Y^2]=\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(t_i,t_j)$.
The number $\mathbb{E}[Y^2]$ is nonnegative, so the sum is nonnegative.
Also $K(s,t)=K(t,s)$, so $K$ is a symmetric [positive definite kernel](c:positive-definite-kernel).
links.why: It shows that every covariance function is a positive definite kernel, so kernel methods apply to it.

reminder: A creation operator adds one particle to a state, and its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator), the annihilation operator, removes one.
definition: On the [Fock space](c:fock-space) $\mathcal F(H)$ of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, the creation operator $a^\dagger(f)$ of a vector $f\in H$ maps an $n$-particle state to an $(n+1)$-particle state by adding a particle in the state $f$, and the annihilation operator $a(f)$ is its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator). They satisfy the [commutator](c:commutator) relation $[a(f),a^\dagger(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle$ for bosons, and the same relation with the anticommutator for fermions.
examples: For the [quantum harmonic oscillator](c:quantum-harmonic-oscillator), $a|n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle$ and $a^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle$.
The number operator is $N=a^\dagger a$, and it satisfies $N|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$.

Non-example: in units with $\hbar=m=\omega=1$, the position operator $x=(a+a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$ is neither a creation nor an annihilation operator, because it changes the particle number by $+1$ and by $-1$.

reminder: The cube root of a real number $x$ is the unique real number $y$ with $y^3=x$.
definition: The cube root is the function $\sqrt[3]{\cdot}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ that sends each [real number](c:real-number) $x$ to the unique real number $y$ with $y^3=x$. It is a continuous, increasing [bijection](c:bijection), the [inverse function](c:inverse-function) of $y\mapsto y^3$, and it is defined for negative $x$ too.
examples: For $x\ge0$, the cube root equals the power $x^{1/3}$.
Non-example: the equation $y^3=1$ has two more solutions $e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$ in $\mathbb{C}$, but they are not the real cube root of $1$.

steps: Take the real $n$th root function, which sends $x$ to the real number $y$ with $y^n=x$.
Choose $n=3$, an odd number.
For odd $n$ the map $y\mapsto y^n$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$, so the root exists for every real $x$.
The result is the cube root.
links.why: It shows that the cube root is the odd case of the real nth root, defined on all of the real line.

reminder: A cubic curve is a curve in the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) cut out by one homogeneous equation of degree three.
definition: A plane cubic curve over a field $k$ is the subscheme of the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) $\mathbb{P}^2_k$ defined by a nonzero homogeneous [polynomial](c:polynomial) $F(x,y,z)$ of degree $3$. Over a [scheme](c:scheme) $S$, a cubic curve is a scheme $X\to S$ with a [section](c:section) $e:S\to X$ such that, Zariski locally on $S$, $X$ is given in $\mathbb{P}^2_S$ by a cubic equation.
examples: The curve $y^2z=x^3-xz^2$ is a smooth cubic, and it is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) with $e=[0:1:0]$.
The curve $y^2z=x^3+x^2z$ is a cubic with a node at $[0:0:1]$, and $y^2z=x^3$ is a cubic with a cusp.
Non-example: the conic $x^2+y^2=z^2$ has degree $2$, so it is not a cubic curve, and a line has degree $1$.

steps: Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a field $k$ with origin $e$.
By the Riemann-Roch theorem, $E$ embeds in $\mathbb{P}^2_k$ as a Weierstrass cubic $y^2z+a_1xyz+a_3yz^2=x^3+a_2x^2z+a_4xz^2+a_6z^3$ with $e=[0:1:0]$.
So $E$ is a cubic curve with the section $e$.
The elliptic case adds that the cubic is smooth.
links.why: It shows that an elliptic curve is a smooth cubic curve with a chosen point.

reminder: The curvature form of a [connection](c:connection) is a 2-form that measures how far covariant derivatives fail to commute.
definition:
For a [connection](c:connection-on-a-vector-bundle) $
abla$ on a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$, the curvature form $F_
abla$ is the $\mathrm{End}(E)$-valued 2-form with $F_
abla(X,Y)s=
abla_X
abla_Ys-
abla_Y
abla_Xs-
abla_{[X,Y]}s$ for [vector fields](c:vector-field) $X,Y$ and sections $s$. In a local frame with connection matrix $A$, it is $F=dA+A\wedge A$, and the connection is called flat when $F=0$.
examples: A [flat connection](c:flat-connection), such as the trivial connection $d$ on a trivial bundle, has $F=0$.
For a line bundle with local connection form $A$, the curvature form is $F=dA$, which is the field strength in electromagnetism.
Non-example: the local connection form $A$ is not the curvature form, because $A$ changes by a derivative term under a change of frame, while $F$ only changes by conjugation.

steps: Take the tangent bundle $TM$ of a Riemannian manifold with its [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection).
The curvature form of this connection is an $\mathrm{End}(TM)$-valued 2-form $F$.
Evaluating $F(X,Y)Z$ gives the Riemann curvature tensor $R(X,Y)Z$.
So Riemann curvature is the curvature form of one particular connection.
links.why: It shows that Riemann curvature is a special case of the curvature of a connection on any bundle.

steps: Start with a connection $\nabla$ on a vector bundle, with curvature form $F_\nabla$.
Add the condition $F_\nabla=0$.
Then $\nabla$ is a [flat connection](c:flat-connection).
links.why: It shows that flatness is exactly the vanishing of the curvature form.

reminder: A CW-spectrum is a [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) of pointed [CW complexes](c:cw-complex) whose structure maps are inclusions of [subcomplexes](c:subcomplex).
definition: A [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) $E$ is a sequence of pointed spaces $E_n$ with structure maps $\sigma_n:\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}$, where $\Sigma$ is the reduced [suspension](c:suspension). It is a CW-spectrum when every $E_n$ is a pointed [CW complex](c:cw-complex) and every $\sigma_n$ is the inclusion of a [subcomplex](c:subcomplex) of $E_{n+1}$.
examples: The [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) $S$ with $S_n=S^n$ is a CW-spectrum.
For a pointed CW complex $X$, the [suspension spectrum](c:suspension-spectrum) $\Sigma^\infty X$ with $(\Sigma^\infty X)_n=\Sigma^nX$ is a CW-spectrum.
Non-example: take $E_n=S^n$ with each $\sigma_n:S^{n+1}\to S^{n+1}$ of degree $2$; the spaces are CW complexes, but $\sigma_n$ is not injective, so it is not an inclusion of a subcomplex.

steps: Let $E$ be a CW-spectrum, with spaces $E_n$ and structure maps $\sigma_n$.
Forget the cell structures: each $E_n$ is still a pointed space, and each $\sigma_n$ is still a map $\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}$.
This data is a [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum).
The CW case adds that each $E_n$ is a CW complex and each $\sigma_n$ includes a subcomplex.
links.why: It shows that a CW-spectrum is a sequential spectrum with cell structures that fit together.

steps: Let $X$ be a pointed CW complex and put $E_n=\Sigma^nX$.
Each $E_n$ is a pointed CW complex, because the suspension of a CW complex is a CW complex.
Take $\sigma_n$ to be the identity $\Sigma E_n=E_{n+1}$, which includes all of $E_{n+1}$ as a subcomplex.
So the [suspension spectrum](c:suspension-spectrum) of $X$ is a CW-spectrum.
links.why: It shows that every suspension spectrum of a CW complex is a CW-spectrum.

reminder: A cyclic quadrilateral is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) whose four vertices lie on one [circle](c:circle).
definition: A [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$ is cyclic when its four vertices lie on a single [circle](c:circle). For a convex quadrilateral, this is equivalent to the condition that its opposite [angles](c:angle) sum to $180^\circ$.
examples: Every rectangle is cyclic, because its diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so their midpoint is equally far from all four vertices.
Every isosceles trapezoid is cyclic.
Non-example: a rhombus that is not a square is not cyclic, because its opposite angles are equal and do not sum to $180^\circ$ unless they are right angles.

steps: Take a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ and forget the circle through its vertices.
What remains is a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) with four vertices and four sides.
The cyclic case adds one condition: the four vertices are [concyclic](c:concyclic-points).
links.why: It shows that a cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral with one extra condition on its vertices.

steps: Start with a [rectangle](c:rectangle) $ABCD$ and let $O$ be the midpoint of its diagonals.
The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so $OA=OB=OC=OD$.
So the four vertices lie on the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$.
Hence every rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral, and the rectangle adds that all four angles are right angles.
links.why: It shows that every rectangle, and so every square, is cyclic.

reminder: The cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$ is the monic [polynomial](c:polynomial) whose roots are exactly the primitive $n$th [roots of unity](c:root-of-unity).
definition: The $n$th cyclotomic polynomial is $\Phi_n(x)=\prod(x-e^{2\pi ik/n})$, the product over $1\le k\le n$ with $\gcd(k,n)=1$, so its roots are the [primitive roots of unity](c:is-primitive-root) of order $n$. It is a monic [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $\varphi(n)$ with integer coefficients, where $\varphi$ is [Euler's totient function](c:euler-s-totient-function), and $x^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)$.
examples: For a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$, $\Phi_p=x^{p-1}+\cdots+x+1$.
Non-example: $x^4-1$ is not $\Phi_4$, because it also has the roots $1$ and $-1$, which are not primitive $4$th roots of unity.

steps: Let $\zeta$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity, so $\Phi_n$ is monic with integer coefficients and $\Phi_n(\zeta)=0$.
The polynomial $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
A monic irreducible polynomial that has $\zeta$ as a root is the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $\zeta$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
So $\Phi_n$ is the minimal polynomial of every primitive $n$th root of unity.
links.why: It shows that the degree of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ equals the degree of $\Phi_n$.

reminder: A D-module is a module over the sheaf of differential operators of a smooth variety or complex manifold.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) or a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), and let $\mathcal D_X$ be its [sheaf](c:sheaf) of rings of differential operators, generated by the functions and the [vector fields](c:vector-field). A D-module on $X$ is a sheaf of left [modules](c:module) over $\mathcal D_X$, which is the same as an $\mathcal O_X$-module with an action of vector fields $\xi$ that satisfies $\xi(fm)=\xi(f)m+f\xi m$ and $[\xi,\eta]m=\xi\eta m-\eta\xi m$.
examples: The structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ is a D-module, with vector fields acting by differentiation.
On the affine line, the module $\mathcal D/\mathcal Dx$ is generated by a delta function at the point $0$.
Non-example: on the affine line, the skyscraper module $\mathcal O/(x)$ at $0$ is an $\mathcal O$-module but not a D-module, because $\partial x-x\partial=1$ would force $1$ to act as $0$.

steps: Take the sheaf of rings $\mathcal D_X$ of differential operators on $X$.
A D-module is a sheaf of modules over $\mathcal D_X$.
The D-module case fixes the ring sheaf to be the differential operators.
links.why: It shows that the general theory of sheaves of modules applies to D-modules.

steps: Let $M$ be a holonomic D-module on a smooth variety $X$.
By definition $M$ is a [coherent D-module](c:coherent-d-module), so it is a D-module.
The holonomic case adds that the [characteristic variety](c:characteristic-variety) of $M$ has dimension $\dim X$, the least possible for a nonzero module.
links.why: It shows that holonomic D-modules are the smallest, best behaved D-modules.

reminder: The degree of a [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) of $L$ as a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $K$.
definition: For a [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$, the field $L$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $K$. The degree $[L:K]$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) $\dim_KL$ of this vector space, a natural number or infinity, and for $K\subseteq L\subseteq M$ the tower law says $[M:K]=[M:L][L:K]$.
examples: $[\mathbb{C}:\mathbb{R}]=2$, with basis $1,i$.
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}]=3$, with basis $1,\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{4}$.
Non-example: the number $4$ of elements of $\mathbb{F}_4$ is not the degree $[\mathbb{F}_4:\mathbb{F}_2]$, because the degree counts the elements of a basis, and it is $2$.

steps: Let $L/K$ be a field extension; multiplication by elements of $K$ makes $L$ a vector space over $K$.
The [dimension of a vector space](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) is the size of any basis.
Apply this to $L$ as a $K$-vector space; the result is $[L:K]$.
links.why: It shows that the degree is a dimension, so linear algebra computes it.

reminder: A subgroup of a topological group is dense when every nonempty open set of the group contains one of its elements.
definition: A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$ is dense when its [closure](c:closure) is all of $G$. Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $G$ meets $H$.
examples: The subgroup $\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt2\,\mathbb{Z}$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is dense.
For irrational $\alpha$, the rotations by integer multiples of $2\pi\alpha$ form a dense subgroup of the circle group.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not dense in $\mathbb{R}$, because the open interval $(0.1,0.9)$ does not meet it.

steps: A subgroup $H$ of $G$ is a subset of the underlying space of $G$.
Ask that this subset be a [dense set](c:dense-set), so that its closure is $G$.
A dense subgroup is thus a dense set that is also a subgroup.
links.why: It shows that density arguments for sets apply to subgroups, with the group structure as a bonus.

reminder: The density of a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is the limit of the fraction $|S\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|/n$ as $n$ grows.
definition: The natural density of a [subset](c:subset) $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is $d(S)=\lim_{n\to\infty}|S\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|/n$, when this [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) exists. More generally, a measurable subset $S$ of a [measure space](c:measure-space) $X$ of finite measure has density $\mu(S)/\mu(X)$, the proportion of $X$ that $S$ fills.
examples: The even numbers have density $1/2$, and the multiples of $k$ have density $1/k$.
The prime numbers have density $0$, by the prime number theorem.
Non-example: the set of $n$ with $\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor$ even has no density, because the fraction oscillates between about $1/3$ and $2/3$.

reminder: A [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) satisfies the descending chain condition when every sequence $a_0\ge a_1\ge\cdots$ is eventually constant.
definition: A [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) satisfies the descending chain condition when every [sequence](c:sequence) $a_0\ge a_1\ge a_2\ge\cdots$ in it is eventually constant. An object $B$ of a [category](c:category) satisfies it when the poset of [subobjects](c:subobject) of $B$ does; for a module, this means that every descending chain of submodules stops.
examples: The natural numbers with the usual order satisfy it, because a descending sequence of natural numbers cannot decrease forever.
A finite-dimensional vector space satisfies it on its subspaces, because the dimension is a natural number that drops at each strict step.
Non-example: the ideals $(2)\supsetneq(4)\supsetneq(8)\supsetneq\cdots$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ form a descending chain that never stops, so $\mathbb{Z}$ fails it as a module over itself.

steps: Take a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $(P,\le)$ and let $a<b$ mean $a\le b$ and $a\ne b$.
An infinite strictly descending sequence $a_0>a_1>\cdots$ is an infinite descent for the relation $<$.
A descending sequence that is not eventually constant has infinitely many strict steps, and those steps form a strictly descending sequence.
So the chain condition holds exactly when $<$ is a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation).
links.why: It shows that the chain condition is well-foundedness of the strict order, which gives induction on the poset.

steps: Let $R$ be a ring and let $B=R$ as a module over itself.
The submodules of $R$ are the left ideals of $R$.
The ring $R$ is Artinian when its poset of left ideals satisfies the descending chain condition.
So an Artinian ring is a ring that, as an object, satisfies the descending chain condition.
links.why: It shows that Artinian rings and modules are the cases of this condition for ideals and submodules.

reminder: A DFA reads a word letter by letter, changes state by a fixed rule, and accepts when it ends in an accepting state.
definition: A deterministic finite automaton over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is a quadruple $(Q,\delta,q_0,F)$ of a set $Q$ of states, which is [finite](c:finite-set) in the classical definition, a transition function $\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q$, a start state $q_0\in Q$ and a set $F\subseteq Q$ of accepting states. It accepts a [word](c:word) $a_1\cdots a_n$ when the states $q_i=\delta(q_{i-1},a_i)$ end with $q_n\in F$, and the set of accepted words is its [language](c:language).
examples: The automaton with states even and odd over $\{0,1\}$ that flips its state on each $1$ accepts the words with an even number of $1$s.
The words over $\{a,b\}$ that end in $ab$ form the language of a DFA with three states.
Non-example: a machine with two transitions $q\xrightarrow{a}q_1$ and $q\xrightarrow{a}q_2$ is nondeterministic, so it is not a DFA, because $\delta(q,a)$ must be a single state.

steps: Let $(Q,\delta,q_0,F)$ be a DFA over $\Sigma$.
Define a transition relation by $\delta'(q,a)=\{\delta(q,a)\}$, a set with exactly one state.
The automaton with this relation accepts a word exactly when the DFA does, because it has only one run on each word.
So every DFA is an [NFA](c:nfa), and the deterministic case adds that each state and letter have exactly one next state.
links.why: It shows that every result about nondeterministic automata also holds for DFAs.

reminder: A differential operator sends a function $u$ to a function whose value at $x$ depends only on the derivatives of $u$ at $x$.
definition: A differential operator of order at most $k$ on sections of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ is a map $D$ with $(Du)(x)=\Phi(x,u(x),\partial u(x),\dots,\partial^ku(x))$, that is, a bundle map $\Phi$ applied to the $k$-[jet](c:jet-bundle) of $u$ at $x$. It is linear when $\Phi$ is linear in the jet variables, and then $D=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}a_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha$ in coordinates.
examples: The derivative $d/dx$ and the Laplacian $\Delta=\sum_i\partial^2/\partial x_i^2$ are linear differential operators.
The map $u\mapsto u_t+uu_x$ is a nonlinear differential operator of order $1$.
Non-example: the integration operator $u\mapsto\int_0^xu(t)\,dt$ is not a differential operator, because its value at $x$ depends on $u$ away from $x$, not only on the jet of $u$ at $x$.

steps: Take a [linear differential operator](c:linear-differential-operator) $D=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}a_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha$.
Its value $(Du)(x)$ depends only on the derivatives of $u$ at $x$ up to order $k$.
So $D$ has the form $\Phi(x,\mathrm{jet}^ku(x))$ with $\Phi$ linear in the jet variables.
Hence $D$ is a differential operator, and the linear case adds that $\Phi$ is linear.
links.why: It shows that linear operators are the special case in which the dependence on the jet is linear.

reminder: A directed graph is a set of [vertices](c:vertex) with a set of arcs, each arc being an [ordered pair](c:ordered-pair) of vertices.
definition: A directed graph, also called a digraph or quiver, is a pair $(V,A)$ of a [set](c:set) $V$ of [vertices](c:vertex) and a set $A\subseteq V\times V$ of arcs, which are [ordered pairs](c:ordered-pair) $(u,v)$ read as arrows from $u$ to $v$. Some authors allow several arcs with the same ends, and then $A$ comes with maps $s,t:A\to V$.
examples: The vertices $\{1,2,3\}$ with the arcs $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,1)$ form a directed 3-cycle.
On $\{1,\dots,n\}$, put an arc $(a,b)$ when $a$ divides $b$.
Non-example: $V=\{1,2,3\}$ with $A=\{(1,4)\}$ is not a directed graph, because $4$ is not a vertex.

steps: Start with a [graph](c:graph) with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$ of unordered pairs $\{u,v\}$.
Replace each edge $\{u,v\}$ by the two arcs $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$.
The result is a directed graph whose arc set is symmetric.
So a graph is a directed graph whose arc set is symmetric.
links.why: It shows that an undirected graph is a directed graph in which every arc has a reverse.

reminder: The directional derivative of $f$ at $x$ along $v$ is the rate of change of $f$ when $x$ moves in the direction $v$.
definition: Let $f$ be a function on an open subset of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), let $x$ be a point and let $v$ be a vector. The directional derivative of $f$ at $x$ along $v$ is $D_vf(x)=\frac{d}{dt}f(x+tv)\big|_{t=0}=\lim_{t\to0}(f(x+tv)-f(x))/t$, the [derivative](c:derivative) of $t\mapsto f(x+tv)$ at $0$, when this [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) exists.
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2y$ at $(1,2)$ along $v=(1,1)$, the directional derivative is $2xy+x^2=5$.
Along a basis vector $e_i$, the directional derivative is the [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) $\partial f/\partial x_i$.
Non-example: for $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$ along $v=1$, the quotient $|t|/t$ is $1$ for $t>0$ and $-1$ for $t<0$, so there is no directional derivative.

steps: Take a function $f$ of $n$ variables and a point $x$.
Choose the direction $v=e_i$, the $i$th basis vector.
Then $f(x+te_i)$ changes only the $i$th variable, so $D_{e_i}f(x)$ is the derivative of $f$ in $x_i$ with the others fixed.
This is the [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) $\partial f/\partial x_i$.
links.why: It shows that partial derivatives are directional derivatives along the coordinate axes.

steps: Take a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and the direction $v=1$.
Then the function $t\mapsto f(x+tv)$ is the function $t\mapsto f(x+t)$.
The derivative of $t\mapsto f(x+t)$ at $t=0$ is $f'(x)$.
So $D_1f(x)$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) of $f$ at $x$.
links.why: It shows that the ordinary derivative is the one-variable case of the directional derivative.

reminder: In the discrete topology on a set, every subset is open.
definition: The discrete topology on a set $X$ is the [topology](c:topology) in which every [subset](c:subset) of $X$ is an [open set](c:open-set). Then every singleton is open, and every map from $X$ to a [topological space](c:topological-space) is continuous.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ with the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}$ are discrete, because $\{n\}=\mathbb{Z}\cap(n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)$.
Every set with the metric $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$ has the discrete topology.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ with the usual topology is not discrete, because every open interval around $q$ contains other rationals, so $\{q\}$ is not open.

steps: Put the discrete metric on $X$, with $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$ and $d(x,x)=0$.
The open ball of radius $1/2$ around $x$ is the singleton $\{x\}$.
So every singleton is open, and every subset is a union of singletons.
Hence the [metric topology](c:metric-topology) of this metric is the discrete topology.
links.why: It shows that the discrete topology comes from a metric, so every set is a metrizable space.

reminder: The Dyck language is the set of bracket words in which every opening bracket is closed by its match in the right order.
definition: For $k\ge1$, let $\Sigma_k=\{a_1,\bar a_1,\dots,a_k,\bar a_k\}$ be an alphabet of $k$ pairs of brackets. The Dyck language $D_k$ is the set of [words](c:word) over $\Sigma_k$ that reduce to the empty word by deleting adjacent pairs $a_i\bar a_i$ again and again; it is a [formal language](c:language), and $D_1$ is the set of balanced parentheses.
examples: In $D_1$, with $a$ the opening and $\bar a$ the closing parenthesis, the words $\varepsilon$, $()$, $(())$ and $()()$ belong to the language.
In $D_2$, with the brackets $()$ and $[]$, the word $([])()$ belongs to the language.
Non-example: the word $)($ is not in $D_1$, although it has as many opening as closing brackets, because a closing bracket comes first; the word $([)]$ is not in $D_2$.

steps: Take the grammar with start symbol $S$ and the rules $S\to\varepsilon$ and $S\to a_iS\bar a_iS$ for each $i$.
Each rule has a single nonterminal on its left side, so the grammar is context-free.
It generates exactly the words that reduce to the empty word, that is, the Dyck language $D_k$.
So $D_k$ is a [context-free language](c:context-free-language), with the extra structure of matched brackets.
links.why: It shows that the Dyck language is context-free, and it is the model for nested structure.

reminder: An $E_n$-operad is a [topological operad](c:topological-operad) equivalent to the little $n$-cubes operad, whose $k$th space is like $k$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
definition: The [little cubes operad](c:little-cubes-operad) $\mathcal C_n$ has as its $k$th space the space of $k$ axis-parallel embeddings of the open unit $n$-cube into itself with disjoint images, and composition inserts one configuration into a cube of another. An $E_n$-operad is any [topological operad](c:topological-operad) connected to $\mathcal C_n$ by a zigzag of operad maps that are weak equivalences in every arity.
examples: An $E_1$-operad is equivalent to the [associative operad](c:associative-operad), whose algebras are monoids.
Every [iterated loop space](c:iterated-loop-space) $\Omega^nX$ is an algebra over an $E_n$-operad.

Non-example: the [commutative operad](c:commutative-monoid-operad) has a point as its binary space, while an $E_n$-operad has a binary space equivalent to $S^{n-1}$, so it is not $E_n$ for any finite $n\ge1$.

steps: The space $\mathcal C_n(k)$ is a topological space for each $k$, and the symmetric group permutes the cubes.
Insertion of configurations gives continuous composition maps that are associative and unital.
So $\mathcal C_n$ is an operad in topological spaces, and every $E_n$-operad is one by definition.
links.why: It shows that an $E_n$-operad is a topological operad, so topological operad tools apply.

reminder: The Einstein field equations say that the [Einstein tensor](c:einstein-tensor) of a [spacetime](c:spacetime) metric is proportional to the stress-energy of matter.
definition:
On a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $(M,g)$, the Einstein field equations are $G_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}= rac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu
u}$, where $G_{\mu
u}=R_{\mu
u}- rac12Rg_{\mu
u}$ is the [Einstein tensor](c:einstein-tensor) built from the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) and the [scalar curvature](c:scalar-curvature), $\Lambda$ is the cosmological constant and $T_{\mu
u}$ is the stress-energy tensor of matter. A solution is a metric $g$ together with matter fields that satisfy these equations.
examples: Minkowski space solves the equations with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$.
The [Schwarzschild metric](c:schwarzschild-metric) solves the vacuum equations $G_{\mu\nu}=0$ outside a spherical mass.
Non-example: the product metric $-dt^2+g_{S^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}\times S^2$ is not a vacuum solution with $\Lambda=0$, because its Einstein tensor has the component $G_{tt}=1\ne0$.

reminder: The end $\int_cF(c,c)$ is the universal object with maps to every $F(c,c)$ that agree on each morphism $f:c\to c'$.
definition: Let $F:C^{op}\times C\to D$ be a [bifunctor](c:bifunctor). An end of $F$ is an object $e$ with morphisms $p_c:e\to F(c,c)$ for all objects $c$ such that $F(c,f)\circ p_c=F(f,c')\circ p_{c'}$ in $\mathrm{Hom}(e,F(c,c'))$ for every morphism $f:c\to c'$, and $e$ is universal with this property. Equivalently, it is a [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of a diagram built from $F$ over the [twisted arrow category](c:twisted-arrow-category) of $C$.
examples: For functors $G,H:C\to D$, the end of $\mathrm{Hom}_D(G(-),H(-))$ is the set of [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) from $G$ to $H$.
The end of $\mathrm{Hom}_C(-,-)$ is the set of natural endomorphisms of the identity functor, which is the [center of the category](c:center-of-a-category).
Non-example: the product $\prod_cF(c,c)$ is not the end, because it keeps families that fail the compatibility condition on morphisms.

steps: Form the [twisted arrow category](c:twisted-arrow-category) of $C$, whose objects are the morphisms of $C$.
Compose $F$ with the functor from this category to $C^{op}\times C$ that sends $f:c\to c'$ to the pair $(c,c')$.
The end of $F$ is the [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of this composite diagram in $D$.
links.why: It shows that an end is a limit, so it exists whenever the category has the needed limits.

reminder: In a category enriched in abelian groups, the endomorphisms of an object form a ring with composition as multiplication.
definition: Let $M$ be an object of an [Ab-enriched category](c:ab-enriched-category), so that each hom-set is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) and composition is bilinear. The endomorphism ring $\mathrm{End}(M)=\mathrm{Hom}(M,M)$ is a [ring](c:ring) with addition from the hom-group, multiplication by composition, and unit $\mathrm{id}_M$.
examples: For an abelian group $A$, the ring $\mathrm{End}(A)$ of group endomorphisms is an endomorphism ring, and $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
For a vector space $V$ of dimension $n$ over a field $k$, $\mathrm{End}(V)\cong M_n(k)$.
Non-example: the endomorphisms of a non-abelian group $G$ form only a monoid under composition, because the pointwise product of two homomorphisms $G\to G$ is not a homomorphism in general.

steps: Take the category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $k$ and the object $k^n$.
A linear map $k^n\to k^n$ is given by an $n\times n$ matrix, and composition is matrix multiplication.
So $\mathrm{End}(k^n)$ is the ring of $n\times n$ matrices, which is the [matrix ring](c:matrix-ring) over $k$.
links.why: It shows that endomorphism rings extend matrix rings to objects of any Ab-enriched category.

reminder: An energy condition is an inequality that the stress-energy tensor of matter must satisfy, such as a non-negative energy density.
definition: In general relativity on a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold), an energy condition is an inequality on the stress-energy tensor $T$ of the matter fields that holds for all causal vectors. Examples are the null energy condition $T(k,k)\ge0$ for all null vectors $k$, and the weak energy condition $T(u,u)\ge0$ for all timelike vectors $u$. Such conditions are the hypotheses of the singularity theorems.
examples: Dust and radiation satisfy the null and weak energy conditions, because their energy density is non-negative.
A positive cosmological constant satisfies the null and weak energy conditions.
Non-example: a negative cosmological constant has $T(u,u)<0$ for every unit timelike $u$, so it violates the weak energy condition, although it satisfies the null one.

reminder: A pair of vertex sets is $\varepsilon$-regular when every large pair of subsets has almost the same [edge density](c:edge-density) as the whole pair.
definition: Let $G$ be a [graph](c:graph) and let $A,B$ be disjoint sets of vertices, with [edge density](c:edge-density) $d(A,B)=e(A,B)/(|A||B|)$. The pair $(A,B)$ is $\varepsilon$-regular when $|d(A',B')-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $A'\subseteq A$ and $B'\subseteq B$ with $|A'|\ge\varepsilon|A|$ and $|B'|\ge\varepsilon|B|$.
examples: A complete bipartite pair has density $1$ on every pair of subsets, so it is $\varepsilon$-regular for every $\varepsilon$.
A random bipartite graph with edge probability $p$ between two large sets is $\varepsilon$-regular with high probability.

Non-example: split $A=A_1\cup A_2$ and $B=B_1\cup B_2$ into halves, and join $A_1$ to $B_1$ and $A_2$ to $B_2$ completely, with no other edges; then $d(A,B)=1/2$ but $d(A_1,B_1)=1$, so the pair is not $\varepsilon$-regular for $\varepsilon<1/2$.

reminder: A [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) is ergodic when every invariant set has measure $0$ or $1$.
definition: A [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) $T$ of a [probability space](c:probability-measure) $(X,\mu)$ is ergodic when every [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $A$ with $T^{-1}(A)=A$ has $\mu(A)=0$ or $\mu(A)=1$. Equivalently, every $T$-invariant measurable function is constant almost everywhere.
examples: The rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha\pmod1$ of the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is ergodic when $\alpha$ is irrational.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\pmod1$ on $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure is ergodic.
Non-example: the identity map of $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure is not ergodic, because the [invariant set](c:invariant-set) $[0,1/2]$ has measure $1/2$.

steps: Let $T$ be weakly mixing and let $A$ be a measurable set with $T^{-1}A=A$.
Then $\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A)=\mu(A)$ for every $n$.
Weak mixing says that the averages of $|\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A)-\mu(A)^2|$ tend to $0$, so $\mu(A)=\mu(A)^2$.
Hence $\mu(A)$ is $0$ or $1$, and $T$ is ergodic.
links.why: It shows that every weakly mixing map is ergodic, so ergodicity is the weakest of the mixing properties.

reminder: An exact category in the sense of Barr is a [regular category](c:regular-category) in which every internal equivalence relation is a kernel pair.
definition: A category is exact in the sense of Barr when it is a [regular category](c:regular-category) in which every internal equivalence relation is an [effective equivalence relation](c:effective-equivalence-relation). Regular means finite limits, coequalizers of [kernel pairs](c:kernel-pair) and regular epimorphisms stable under pullback; effective means that the relation is the kernel pair of its coequalizer.
examples: The category $\mathrm{Set}$ is exact, because every equivalence relation is the kernel pair of its quotient map.
Every [abelian category](c:abelian-category) and every [topos](c:topos) is exact.
Non-example: the category $\mathrm{Top}$ is not exact, because it is not even regular: the pullback of a quotient map need not be a quotient map.

steps: Let $C$ be an exact category.
By definition $C$ is regular: it has finite limits, coequalizers of kernel pairs and pullback-stable regular epimorphisms.
The exact case adds that every internal equivalence relation in $C$ is the kernel pair of its coequalizer.
links.why: It shows that exact categories keep every property of regular categories and add effective quotients.

steps: Let $A$ be an [abelian category](c:abelian-category), so it has finite limits and every epimorphism is a cokernel.
Every epimorphism is regular, and the pullback of an epimorphism is an epimorphism, so $A$ is regular.
An equivalence relation $R\rightarrowtail X\times X$ in $A$ is the kernel pair of the quotient $X\to X/R$.
So every internal equivalence relation is effective, and $A$ is exact.
links.why: It shows that Barr-exactness is the part of abelian category theory that works without addition.

reminder: The exterior algebra of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is the algebra generated by $V$ with $v\wedge v=0$ for every $v$.
definition: The exterior algebra $\Lambda(V)$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $k$ is the quotient of the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) $T(V)$ by the two-sided [ideal](c:ideal) generated by all $v\otimes v$. It is an [algebra over a field](c:algebra-over-a-field) graded by degree, $\Lambda(V)=\bigoplus_p\Lambda^pV$, with a product $\wedge$ that satisfies $v\wedge w=-w\wedge v$ for $v,w\in V$.
examples: If $V=k^n$ has basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$, then $\Lambda(V)$ has the basis $e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}$ with $i_1<\cdots<i_p$, so its dimension is $2^n$.
For $V=\mathbb{R}^3$, the degrees $0,1,2,3$ of $\Lambda(V)$ have dimensions $1,3,3,1$.
Non-example: the polynomial algebra $k[x,y]$, which is the [symmetric algebra](c:symmetric-algebra) of $k^2$, is not an exterior algebra, because $xy=yx$ and $x^2\ne0$ there.

steps: Take the exterior algebra $\Lambda(V)$ with its pieces $\Lambda^pV$.
The product sends $\Lambda^pV\times\Lambda^qV$ into $\Lambda^{p+q}V$.
So $\Lambda(V)$ is a [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra).
The exterior case adds that homogeneous generators of degree one anticommute and have square zero.
links.why: It shows that the exterior algebra is a graded algebra with a sign rule for its product.

reminder: The exterior covariant derivative extends a connection to [differential forms](c:differential-form) with values in a vector bundle.
definition:
Let $
abla$ be a [covariant derivative](c:covariant-derivative) on a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$. The exterior covariant derivative $d_
abla:\Omega^p(M;E)	o\Omega^{p+1}(M;E)$ is the operator with $d_
abla=
abla$ on sections and $d_
abla(\omega\otimes s)=d\omega\otimes s+(-1)^p\omega\wedge
abla s$ for a $p$-form $\omega$ and a section $s$, built from the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d$. Its square $d_
abla^2$ is multiplication by the curvature of $
abla$.
examples: On sections, which are the case $p=0$, the operator $d_\nabla$ is the covariant derivative $\nabla$.
On the trivial bundle $M\times\mathbb{R}^r$ with the trivial connection, $d_\nabla$ is $d$ applied to each component.
For a line bundle with local connection form $A$, $d_\nabla\omega=d\omega+A\wedge\omega$.
Non-example: applying $d$ to the local components of a bundle-valued form is not well defined for a nontrivial bundle, because the result changes under a change of frame.

steps: Take the trivial line bundle $E=M\times\mathbb{R}$ with the trivial connection $\nabla=d$.
A form with values in $E$ is an ordinary differential form $\omega$, written $\omega\otimes1$.
Since $\nabla1=0$, the formula gives $d_\nabla(\omega\otimes1)=d\omega\otimes1$.
So $d_\nabla$ is the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d$ in this case.
links.why: It shows that the exterior derivative is the exterior covariant derivative of the trivial bundle.

reminder: A Fermat prime is a [prime number](c:prime-number) of the form $2^{2^n}+1$.
definition: A Fermat prime is a [prime number](c:prime-number) of the form $F_n=2^{2^n}+1$ for some [natural number](c:natural-number) $n\ge0$. The known Fermat primes are $F_0,\dots,F_4$, that is $3,5,17,257,65537$, and no other is known.
examples: The numbers $F_0=3$, $F_1=5$, $F_2=17$, $F_3=257$ and $F_4=65537$ are Fermat primes.
A regular polygon with a Fermat prime number of sides can be constructed with compass and straightedge.
Non-example: $F_5=2^{32}+1=4294967297=641\times6700417$ is not prime, and $7$ is prime but not of the form $2^{2^n}+1$.

steps: Take a Fermat prime $p=2^{2^n}+1$.
By definition $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
The Fermat case adds that $p-1$ is the power of two $2^{2^n}$.
links.why: It shows that a Fermat prime is a prime of very special shape, so $p-1$ has no odd factor.

steps: Take the [Fermat numbers](c:fermat-number) $F_n=2^{2^n}+1$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$.
Keep only those $F_n$ that are prime.
These are the Fermat primes, so every Fermat prime is a Fermat number.
links.why: It shows that Fermat primes are the prime members of the Fermat numbers.

reminder: Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it, starting from $F_0=0$ and $F_1=1$.
definition: The Fibonacci numbers form the [sequence](c:sequence) of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $F_n$ defined by $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and the [recurrence relation](c:recurrence-relation) $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$.
examples: Binet's formula gives $F_n=(\varphi^n-\psi^n)/\sqrt5$, with $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $\psi=(1-\sqrt5)/2$.
Non-example: the Lucas numbers $2,1,3,4,7,11,\dots$ obey the same recurrence but start with $L_0=2$ and $L_1=1$, so they are not the Fibonacci numbers.

steps: Write the rule as $F_n=1\cdot F_{n-1}+1\cdot F_{n-2}$ with constant coefficients.
A sequence with $x_n=c_1x_{n-1}+c_2x_{n-2}$ for fixed numbers $c_1,c_2$ obeys a [linear recurrence](c:linear-recurrence) of order $2$.
Take $c_1=c_2=1$ and the start values $0$ and $1$.
The result is the Fibonacci sequence.
links.why: It shows that the general solution method for linear recurrences gives Binet's formula.

reminder: A family of sets has the finite intersection property when every finite subfamily has a nonempty [intersection](c:intersection).
definition: A family $\mathcal F$ of [subsets](c:subset) of a [set](c:set) $X$ has the finite intersection property when the [intersection](c:intersection) of every [finite set](c:finite-set) of members of $\mathcal F$ is nonempty.
examples: The sets $[0,1/n]$ for $n\ge1$ have the property, because every finite intersection equals $[0,1/N]$ for the largest $n=N$ in it, which is nonempty.
In a [compact space](c:compact-space), every family of closed sets with the property has a nonempty intersection.
Non-example: the sets $\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$ and $\{1,3\}$ meet two at a time, but $\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}\cap\{1,3\}=\emptyset$, so the family lacks the property.

steps: Take a [filter](c:filter) $\mathcal F$ on $X$ and finitely many members $F_1,\dots,F_n$ of it.
A filter is closed under finite intersections, so $F_1\cap\cdots\cap F_n$ belongs to $\mathcal F$.
A filter does not contain the empty set, so this intersection is nonempty.
So every filter has the finite intersection property, and the filter adds closure under finite intersections and supersets.
links.why: It shows that a family with the property generates a filter, so it is a starting point for ultrafilter arguments.
